course_title: Essentials of Chinese Language in Social Life
course_description:
This course is designed for students who speak Mandarin Chinese as their first language and for students who are studying advanced Mandarin Chinese in Australia. The course covers language issues related to policy, place, history, ideology, and social practice that concern users of Mandarin Chinese in everyday life.

This course has a maximum quota of 600 students and enrolment will be granted to the first 600 students who enrol via mySI-net. Please note, the maximum quota is for the Semester 2 2026 offering only.

In this course, we will explore the personal and social meaning of using Chinese in the lives of multilingual and multicultural people. We will analyse and discuss language use by people with various backgrounds, experiences, and histories. These will include language data about growing up in multilingual families, migration in childhood and adulthood, voluntary learning of Chinese as a second language during study abroad, commodifying Chinese language in the tourism industry in Kathmandu, and describing people with mental illness in news articles. Along the way, we will encounter inspiring stories, tragic stories, nutty stories, and tender stories. In these stories, we will develop a new understanding of the relationship between language, cultural, and personal identity in a multilingual and multicultural world.

course_aims: The course covers language issues related to policy, place, history, ideology and social practice that concern users of Mandarin Chinese in everyday life. It aims to help students understand why and how language use is simultaneously social and individual choices. Students will be guided through analysing language use in different social settings of their everyday lives, which helps students develop linguistic and intercultural skills valued in their future workplace and by employers alike.

learning_outcomes.description: Analyse the form, meaning, and function of languages with regard to their contexts in everyday life, including workplace interactions.
Develop a comprehensive understanding of the historical development of Chinese languages.
Understand its social and regional variances.
Become a skillful user of languages and an intercultural communicator.
Demonstrate respect for cultural and social diversity and for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and perspectives.
Demonstrate knowledge and respect for ethics and ethical standards in completing assessment tasks.
Lead self and others in group activities.
Be confident dealing with ambiguity and uncertainty.
Present persuasive oral and written arguments.
Be empathetic of other people, cultures, and knowledge systems.

assessment_details.task_description: CHIN2600 Project 1: In-Class English Presentation Purposes: Identify a real-world and language-centered problem. Use the theories or concepts learned in class to explain the problem. Communicate your preliminary findings to others in English, particularly to those unfamiliar with Chinese language and culture. Preparation for the final project. Due Date: Week 7 – Week 9 in class Weight: 60 % Task Description: Present to others in English how the theories/concepts you have learned from CHIN2600 can be used to explain a problem in your social life. You are highly encouraged to develop this project into your final project. Details: You will need to identify a research topic about real-world, language-based problems; explain why it is a problem by including all aspects; justify why the problems are critical by reviewing existing discussions; connect the problems to an aspect of Chinese language discussed in the class; explain which theory or concept taught in class can better explain the problems; collect some “social interactional” data to illustrate the problem (e.g., recordings of social interactions or online discussion); use concepts/theories taught in class to analyse an example from the data; and present your findings. Overall, you should make extensive research on your topic and show your understanding in the presentation with multiple sources. Make your presentation engaging and insightful. When collecting and analysing language data, always start with a social relationship or identity and then explore related language features, rather than the other way around. Format: The presentation is in-person and in-class and should last no longer than 6 minutes. Please use a PowerPoint presentation or any visual aids to present your project. If you are using PowerPoint, include only keywords or phrases on the slides, not sentences from your script. Avoid simply reading from slides during the presentation. You may use a palm card or note to help you deliver the presentation, but if you aim for higher marks, you should avoid using any of them to demonstrate that you can improvise without being constrained by the script. You will find that this helps you speak more naturally because you give more attention to the audience. Your time limit is 6 minutes, and a minimum of 5 minutes and 40 seconds. Make sure you stay within this timeframe. The presentation will be followed by a 3-minute question-and-answer session with the instructor and potentially classmates. The Q&A session covers all course readings and lecutre material. Presentation schedule: To be announced on Blackboard during Week 4. Submission: Upload your PowerPoint slides to Blackboard (CHIN2600 Blackboard > Assessment > In-Class English Presentation > PowerPoint Slides Submission) the day before your presentation. What to include in your presentation: What is your topic? Why is it an important problem according to the existing discussions in news media, government policy, or AI search? What theories or concepts taught in the class can be used to better understand the problem? Why? Use the theories or concepts taught in the class to analyze at least one illustrative example. Language: English Length: 6-minute presentation + 3-minute Q&A Presentation schedule: To be announced on Blackboard during Week 4 Assessment criteria: Demonstrate understanding of theories or concepts discussed in the class and be able to use them to explain a real-world and language-based problem in social life Clear, coherent expression, engaging presentation style Effective use of visuals/multimedia/Powerpoint Check the rubric on Blackboard for more details STATEMENT ON GENERATIVE AI & MT Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Translation (MT) are emerging tools that may support students in completing this assessment task. Students may appropriately use AI and/or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly reference any use of AI or MT in each instance. A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Project 2: Final Chinese Video
assessment_details.due_date: 9/11/2026 3:00 pm Monday, Exam WEEK 1 Submission: Upload your video to Blackboard (CHIN2600 Blackboard > Assessment > Final Chinese Video> Final video submission). You have unlimited attempts to submit before the due date and time.
assessment_details.task_description: CHIN2600 Final Chinese Video Purpose: Synthesize your learning, both theoretical and practical, and propose solutions to the identified problem. Due Date: November 9 at 15:00 pm (Brisbane time) Weight: 40%. Video length: within 10 minutes Description: Create a video analyzing Chinese social interactional data collected from your own social life, and relate your findings to a concept and theory discussed in class. You will also collect English data on a similar phenomenon to compare and contrast with your Chinese data. Use the findings from your analysis to propose solutions to the problem you have identified. You are encouraged to base this video on the problem you identified in your in-class presentation project, though you are welcome to focus on a different topic if you prefer. What to include: The video should have the following components: An introduction that introduces a real-world and language-based problem and the importance of the problem; A theoretical section that briefly explains what theories you are using in analysing the data and why they are the best theories for analysing the data. The theories must be from the readings covered in class; A data section that briefly explains how the Chinese and English data were collected and selected; A data analysis section that presents your analysis with at least four illustrative (2 Chinese and 2 English) examples. This is the main part of the video; A solution section that uses one of the solution approaches taught in class and has at least three suggestions for the identified problem. The suggestions should be based on the findings of the data analysis. This is also the main part of the video; Conclusion section that summarizes your findings; A reference list in the end that includes sources you referenced in the paper. In the reference list, provide the URL to your interview/interactional recordings if you use them as your data. The powerpoint slides should follow APA https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/general_format.html Make sure to relate the analysis to the themes, theoretical frameworks, or concepts studied in class. Your data analysis must include transcripts (interactional data) or texts (screenshots). Transcripts should have Chinese characters (Chinese data) and English words (English data). Upload your slides and video to Blackboard The video needs to show your face and student ID without adding any filters. Submission: Upload your video to Blackboard (CHIN2600 Blackboard > Assessment > Final Chinese Video and Interview > Final video submission). You have unlimited attempts to submit before the due date and time.
